title: Wren and the Lantern
premise: In the river city of Vellmark, 1848, Wendell Nystrom cuts typefaces in her father's print shop while revolution smolders in the streets she refuses to look at. When a census taker records her as a witness to a magistrate's midnight murder of a printer-organizer, Wendell becomes both evidence and target: the magistrate's men begin burning presses, and her father's shop is next. Armed with the dead man's hidden ledger and a stolen printing plate, Wendell must move it past three military checkpoints before the armistice signing either legitimizes the magistrate's power or collapses with the old order. She succeeds at terrible cost — her father dies holding the last checkpoint — and the ledger is printed in ten thousand copies by dawn, forcing the armistice terms to include trials. Wendell learns that history was never happening elsewhere; it was always waiting for someone willing to set its type.
about_author: Cyrus Fairweather is the pen name of a former letterpress compositor who spent fifteen years restoring nineteenth-century print shops across Central Europe. Their novels examine how ordinary tradespeople become unwilling archivists of political violence.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. A routine census visit to the print shop turns sinister when the taker asks whether Wendell saw anything on Ropewalk Lane the night the organizer Tam Voss died. She lies; he writes something anyway. The chapter establishes her deliberate invisibility and ends with the chill of realizing paperwork can be a weapon. Emotional beat: unease beneath domestic routine.

chapters.title: Lead and Memory
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. Flashbacks interleave with present work as she cuts a commemorative typeface, revealing her mother's death during a previous crackdown and why the family chose silence. Her father Augustin burns a bundle of pamphlets rather than be caught with them. Wendell finds one surviving page tucked inside a type drawer — signed by Tam Voss. Emotional beat: grief resurfacing as anger.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Keeps
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The surviving page leads her to Voss's widow, Marta, who reveals a hidden ledger naming Magistrate Corven's death squads and their paymasters. Marta asks Wendell not to take it — then dies in a staged 'accident' two days later. Wendell takes the ledger from under the floorboards as soldiers loot the house. Emotional beat: the moment choice becomes obligation.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. She maps the route to the provisional assembly's press: the Customs Bridge, the Garrison Gate, and the Armory Square checkpoint, each guarded by men loyal to Corven. Augustin, finally awake to the danger, offers his old smuggler contacts. They plan to hide the ledger inside a shipment of type metal. Emotional beat: fear transmuted into methodical resolve.

chapters.title: The First Bridge
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Wendell and a customs sergeant, Brenner, who is corrupt but not murderous. The type-metal ruse nearly fails when a crate is opened; Wendell bluffs that the 'lead' is poisoned scrap from a plague house. Brenner waves them through but marks her face. Emotional beat: vertigo of first transgression — she has crossed a line she cannot uncross.

chapters.title: Corven's Invitation
chapters.summary: Magistrate Corven's POV. He summons Wendell, courteous and terrifying, offering protection and a commission for her father's foundry if she surrenders 'seditious material.' He reveals he knows about Marta. Wendell plays the frightened craftsman's daughter and accepts tea she doesn't drink. Emotional beat: the seduction of safety, and the discovery that power corrupts even its manners.

chapters.title: Garrison Gate
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV. The second crossing goes wrong: Augustin's contact has been arrested, and the gate commander — Corven's protégé Halder — orders every crate stripped. Augustin creates a diversion using the shop's delivery cart and molten type metal, badly burning his hands. Wendell gets the ledger through inside her coat. Emotional beat: love expressed as sacrifice; guilt sharpening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Armistice That Isn't
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs — Halder, an assembly clerk, Wendell. News breaks that Corven has delayed the armistice signing indefinitely, meaning martial law continues and the third checkpoint becomes a killing ground. The assembly clerk, Ilse, tells Wendell the ledger alone won't matter unless thousands read it before Corven consolidates. Emotional beat: despair at the moving finish line.

chapters.title: Armory Square
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, climax. With the press waiting beyond the final checkpoint, Augustin insists on driving the cart himself through Armory Square during the pre-signing procession. Soldiers open fire; Augustin is mortally wounded but the crash scatters printed decoys, chaos swallowing the square while Wendell runs the ledger to Ilse's press on foot. Emotional beat: fury and heartbreak fused into action.

chapters.title: Ten Thousand Copies
chapters.summary: Wendell's POV, resolution. By dawn the ledger is printed and plastered across the city; crowds force the armistice terms to include tribunals, and Corven flees before arrest. At her father's ruined shop, Wendell sets a new typeface — her own design — and prints the first honest census of the dead. She stops hiding. Emotional beat: mourning transformed into authorship; inheritance reclaimed as voice.
